welcome.headline: Every stone here has a secret.
welcome.body: Point your camera at anything. Guess its secret, then find the clue. Takes 30 seconds.

tiles.label: Full ticket
tiles.note: Prices vary by ticket. Check the official site.

sources.title: Finestre sull’Arte: named tickets and 20,000 a day

places.name: Forum
aiDescriptions: the ruins of the Roman Forum of Pompeii with columns and Mount Vesuvius in the background
an open grassy square surrounded by ancient Roman columns and brick ruins

story.question: This big open square was the heart of Roman Pompeii. What happened here?
story.subtitle: This was Pompeii’s forum.
story.body: Temples, the law court and market halls stood around this square, with the Temple of Jupiter at the north end and Vesuvius rising behind it.
story.dinnerLine: “In Pompeii, the main square came with a volcano view.”

sticker.title: Vesuvius from the Forum
sticker.back: Vesuvius rises right behind the Temple of Jupiter.

story.recallPrompt: Remember the big square in Pompeii? What happened there?

sources.title: World History Encyclopedia: Temple of Jupiter, Forum of Pompeii
Wikipedia: Temple of Jupiter (Pompeii)
Board of Cultural Heritage of Pompeii (2015 guide, p. 84)

places.name: House of the Tragic Poet
aiDescriptions: an ancient Roman floor mosaic of a black chained dog with the words CAVE CANEM
a black and white mosaic of a dog at a house entrance in Pompeii

story.eyebrow: House of the Tragic Poet · Pompeii
story.question: The Latin words in this doorway mosaic are a message to visitors. What do they say?
story.subtitle: In Latin: Cave canem.
story.body: The mosaic sits in the entrance floor, so every visitor stepped over a snarling dog on the way in.
story.dinnerLine: Romans had “Beware of the dog” signs too, made of tiny stones.

sticker.title: Beware of the dog
sticker.back: Pompeii’s front doors had “Beware of the dog” in mosaic.

story.recallPrompt: Remember the mosaic in the doorway? What did it warn you about?

sources.title: Wikipedia: House of the Tragic Poet
World History Encyclopedia: Cave Canem dog mosaic
Board of Cultural Heritage of Pompeii (2015 guide, p. 59)

places.name: Thermopolium
aiDescriptions: an ancient Roman stone counter with large round holes for food jars
a painted Roman shrine with gods and two snakes on a red wall

story.question: Romans queued at this counter every day. What was it?
story.subtitle: Romans called it a thermopolium.
story.body: The holes held big jars of hot food and wine, served straight to people in the street. This one belonged to Lucius Vetutius Placidus.

theory.label: THEORY
theory.text: many Romans ate out because small flats had no kitchen.

story.dinnerLine: “Pompeii had fast food almost 2,000 years ago.”

lookCloser.prompt: Behind the counter is a painted shrine. Find the two snakes that guarded the shop.
lookCloser.hint: Tip: look below the painted gods

sticker.title: The guardian snakes
sticker.back: Romans painted snakes by the counter to protect the shop.

story.recallPrompt: Remember yesterday’s stone counter? Was it a bank, a bar or a bakery?

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Romana (University of Chicago): Thermopolium
World History Encyclopedia: Thermopolium of Vetutius Placidus
Athena Review: the lararium and its serpents
Wikipedia: Thermopolium
Board of Cultural Heritage of Pompeii (2015 guide, p. 23)

places.name: Amphitheatre
aiDescriptions: an ancient Roman oval amphitheatre with tiers of stone seats around a sandy arena
the amphitheatre of Pompeii

story.question: Gladiators fought in this arena. Which came first: it, or Rome’s Colosseum?
story.subtitle: Built in the 1st century BC.
story.body: Pompeii’s amphitheatre was built in the first century BC, long before Rome’s Colosseum. It is one of the oldest surviving Roman arenas, and crowds came from the whole region to watch the games.
story.dinnerLine: “Pompeii had a stone arena long before Rome had the Colosseum.”

sticker.title: Older than the Colosseum
sticker.back: Pompeii’s amphitheatre dates from the 1st century BC.

story.recallPrompt: Remember Pompeii’s amphitheatre? Which came first: it or the Colosseum?

sources.title: Board of Cultural Heritage of Pompeii (2015 guide, p. 34)
Wikipedia: Amphitheatre of Pompeii

places.name: Large Theatre
aiDescriptions: a Roman open-air theatre with a semicircle of stone seats built into a slope and a stage building
the Large Theatre of Pompeii

story.question: No great walls hold up these seats. What does?
story.subtitle: The builders used the slope.
story.body: The Large Theatre’s curved seating rests on the natural slope of the ground. Instead of raising a huge structure, Pompeii’s builders let the landscape do the work and turned a hillside into the city’s stage.
story.dinnerLine: “Pompeii’s big theatre sits on a hillside, not on walls.”

sticker.title: Seats on a hill
sticker.back: The Large Theatre’s seats rest on the natural slope.

story.recallPrompt: Remember Pompeii’s Large Theatre? What holds up its seats?

sources.title: Board of Cultural Heritage of Pompeii (2015 guide, p. 113)
Wikipedia (it): Teatro Grande (Pompei)

places.name: Small Theatre (Odeon)
aiDescriptions: a small Roman theatre with a compact half circle of stone seats enclosed by walls
the Small Theatre or Odeon of Pompeii

story.question: Pompeii already had a big theatre next door. What made this small one different?
story.subtitle: A covered hall for smaller audiences.
story.body: Beside the open-air Large Theatre stood this smaller covered theatre. With a roof over its seats, it gave performances a more intimate setting, a very different atmosphere from the big auditorium next door.
story.dinnerLine: “Pompeii had two theatres side by side: one open to the sky, one with a roof.”

sticker.title: The roofed theatre
sticker.back: Pompeii’s small theatre was covered, unlike its big neighbour.

story.recallPrompt: Remember Pompeii’s small theatre? What made it different?

sources.title: Board of Cultural Heritage of Pompeii (2015 guide, p. 115)
Wikipedia: Odeon of Pompeii

places.name: Basilica
clues: A raised platform at the end
aiDescriptions: a large ruined Roman hall with rows of brick column bases and a raised platform at one end
the Basilica of Pompeii beside the Forum

story.question: Long before churches used the name, what happened in a basilica?
story.subtitle: Pompeii’s great public hall.
story.body: Long before the word meant a church, a basilica was a public hall. Beside the Forum, this one hosted legal cases and business deals, the everyday decisions that kept the city running.
story.dinnerLine: “In Pompeii, a basilica was a courthouse, not a church.”

sticker.title: Court and commerce
sticker.back: A Roman basilica hosted trials and business, not worship.

story.recallPrompt: Remember Pompeii’s Basilica? What happened there?

sources.title: Board of Cultural Heritage of Pompeii (2015 guide, p. 105)
Wikipedia (it): Basilica (Pompei)

places.name: Mensa Ponderaria
clues: At the edge of the Forum
aiDescriptions: an ancient stone table with round hollows of different sizes carved into its top
the Mensa Ponderaria measuring table at the Forum of Pompeii

story.question: The hollows in this stone table had one job. What was it?
story.subtitle: The city’s official measuring table.
story.body: Shoppers in Pompeii could check they were not being cheated. This public stone table set the standard measures, so merchants and buyers compared goods against an agreed reference: an ancient answer to a modern problem.
story.dinnerLine: “Pompeii had an official stone table to stop shopkeepers cheating.”

sticker.title: Fair measure
sticker.back: Merchants checked their measures against this public table.

story.recallPrompt: Remember the stone table at the Forum? What were its hollows for?

sources.title: Board of Cultural Heritage of Pompeii (2015 guide, p. 85)
Wikipedia (it): Foro di Pompei

places.name: Castellum Aquae
aiDescriptions: a small square Roman brick water distribution building beside an ancient city gate
the Castellum Aquae water tower of Pompeii

story.question: Pompeii’s aqueduct water arrived at this high point. What happened to it next?
answers: It was stored for fighting fires
It was sold by the jug
It was split into pipes across town
story.subtitle: Pipes branched to every district.
story.body: Aqueduct water reached Pompeii at this building on the town’s highest ground. From here it was channelled into a branching network of pipes and carried down to different parts of the city.
story.dinnerLine: “Pompeii’s water was shared out from one building at the top of town.”

sticker.title: Water for the city
sticker.back: Aqueduct water was split here into pipes across Pompeii.

story.recallPrompt: Remember Pompeii’s water building? What happened to the water there?

sources.title: Board of Cultural Heritage of Pompeii (2015 guide, p. 69)
Wikipedia (it): Castellum Aquae

places.name: Central Baths
aiDescriptions: unfinished Roman bath walls of brick and stone around a large open courtyard
the Central Baths of Pompeii

story.question: These huge baths look unfinished. Why?
answers: They were still being built in AD 79
story.subtitle: The eruption stopped the work.
story.body: The Central Baths were still being built when Vesuvius erupted in AD 79. Their unfinished walls freeze a Roman building site in mid-work, as clearly as any finished monument in the city.
story.dinnerLine: “Pompeii’s newest baths were never finished. Vesuvius got there first.”

sticker.title: Never finished
sticker.back: The Central Baths were a building site when Vesuvius erupted.

story.recallPrompt: Remember the Central Baths? Why do they look unfinished?

sources.title: Board of Cultural Heritage of Pompeii (2015 guide, p. 123)

places.name: Stabian Baths
aiDescriptions: a Roman bath complex with an exercise courtyard surrounded by columns and vaulted bathing rooms
the Stabian Baths of Pompeii

story.question: For Pompeians, the baths were about more than washing. What else?
story.subtitle: Rooms at different temperatures.
story.body: These baths combined rooms at different temperatures with spaces for exercise and conversation. For Pompeians, the daily bath was also the chance to work out, catch up and meet other people.
story.dinnerLine: “For Romans, the baths were the gym, the spa and the café in one.”

sticker.title: The daily bath
sticker.back: Pompeians bathed, exercised and socialised here.

story.recallPrompt: Remember the Stabian Baths? What were they for, besides washing?

sources.title: Board of Cultural Heritage of Pompeii (2015 guide, p. 95)
Wikipedia: Stabian Baths

places.name: House of Octavius Quartio
aiDescriptions: a Roman town house garden with a long water channel lined with plants and a pergola
the garden of the House of Octavius Quartio in Pompeii

story.question: Its owners wanted a country villa in the middle of town. What did they build?
story.subtitle: A country villa inside the city.
story.body: Long water channels and landscaped gardens gave this town house the feel of a countryside villa. Its owners created a corner of leisure inside Pompeii’s crowded street grid.
story.dinnerLine: “One Pompeii family built a country garden with waterways right in the middle of town.”

sticker.title: Villa in the city
sticker.back: Garden waterways turned a town house into a country villa.

story.recallPrompt: Remember the House of Octavius Quartio? What made it feel like a country villa?

sources.title: Board of Cultural Heritage of Pompeii (2015 guide, p. 30)
Wikipedia: House of Loreius Tiburtinus

places.name: House of the Vettii
aiDescriptions: a richly painted Roman house with red and black frescoed walls around a garden courtyard with columns
the House of the Vettii in Pompeii

story.question: The owners of this lavish house had an unusual past. What was it?
story.subtitle: Two freedmen who became rich.
story.body: Two prosperous freedmen, former slaves, owned this richly painted house. Its decoration, including a figure of Priapus as a symbol of prosperity, showed off their success in a city where status could change.
story.dinnerLine: “One of Pompeii’s most lavish houses belonged to two former slaves.”

sticker.title: Freedmen’s fortune
sticker.back: The Vettii brothers rose from slavery to wealth.

story.recallPrompt: Remember the House of the Vettii? What was unusual about its owners?

sources.title: Board of Cultural Heritage of Pompeii (2015 guide, p. 66)
Wikipedia: House of the Vettii

places.name: House of the Faun
clues: A mosaic welcome at the door
aiDescriptions: a large Roman house atrium with a shallow pool and a small bronze statue of a dancing faun
the House of the Faun in Pompeii

story.question: A giant floor mosaic in this house showed a battle. Whose?
story.subtitle: The famous Alexander Mosaic.
story.body: This vast house once held the famous Alexander Mosaic, along with the small dancing faun that gives it its name. Its art and size show how rich Pompeians used their homes to impress guests.
story.dinnerLine: “The famous Alexander Mosaic was once the floor of a Pompeii house.”

sticker.title: The dancing faun
sticker.back: This house held the Alexander Mosaic and a dancing faun.

story.recallPrompt: Remember the House of the Faun? Whose battle did its great mosaic show?

sources.title: Board of Cultural Heritage of Pompeii (2015 guide, p. 56)
Wikipedia: House of the Faun

places.name: Villa of the Mysteries
aiDescriptions: a Roman room painted with a continuous frieze of life-size figures on a deep red background
the Villa of the Mysteries outside Pompeii

story.question: Life-size figures on red walls take part in a secret rite. For which god?
story.subtitle: What the rite means is still debated.
story.body: One continuous painted frieze wraps around a room here, showing figures in a ritual linked to Dionysus. Experts still debate exactly what it shows, which keeps this villa one of Pompeii’s great puzzles.

theory.label: THEORY
theory.text: it shows a young woman’s initiation before marriage.

story.dinnerLine: “Nobody is sure what the Villa of the Mysteries frescoes really show.”

sticker.title: The secret rite
sticker.back: A painted frieze of a rite linked to Dionysus.

story.recallPrompt: Remember the Villa of the Mysteries? Which god is its rite linked to?

sources.title: Board of Cultural Heritage of Pompeii (2015 guide, p. 77)
Wikipedia: Villa of the Mysteries

places.name: Lupanar
aiDescriptions: a narrow Roman building on a corner of two stone streets with small rooms inside
the Lupanar of Pompeii

story.question: Tiny rooms and walls full of writing. What was this building?
story.subtitle: Its walls still carry inscriptions.
story.body: Small rooms and surviving wall inscriptions identify this building as a brothel. It is difficult evidence, often linked to slavery, about the lives of people that history rarely remembers.
story.dinnerLine: “Pompeii’s brothel walls still carry messages written by people almost 2,000 years ago.”

sticker.title: Walls that talk
sticker.back: Inscriptions survive on the walls of Pompeii’s brothel.

story.recallPrompt: Remember the building with tiny rooms and writing on the walls? What was it?

sources.title: Board of Cultural Heritage of Pompeii (2015 guide, p. 97)
Wikipedia: Lupanar

places.name: House of Casca Longus
aiDescriptions: a Roman house atrium with a marble table on carved legs and small painted theatre scenes
the House of Casca Longus in Pompeii

story.question: A marble table here carries a name linked to a famous murder. Which one?
story.subtitle: The table names Casca Longus.
story.body: A marble table found here bears the name of Publius Servilius Casca Longus, linked to one of the men who killed Julius Caesar in 44 BC. Roman politics, carved into the furniture of a Pompeian home.
story.dinnerLine: “A table in Pompeii carries a name linked to Caesar’s assassins.”

sticker.title: Caesar’s shadow
sticker.back: A table here names Casca Longus, linked to Caesar’s killers.

story.recallPrompt: Remember the marble table in Pompeii? Which murder is its name linked to?

sources.title: Board of Cultural Heritage of Pompeii (2015 guide, p. 15)
Wikipedia (it): Casa dei Quadretti Teatrali

places.name: House of the Moralist
aiDescriptions: a Roman dining room with painted walls and short lines of Latin writing
the House of the Moralist in Pompeii

story.question: Painted lines in this dining room give guests advice. About what?
answers: How to pay for the meal
story.subtitle: House rules, painted on the walls.
story.body: Painted sayings around this home’s dining area told guests how to behave at banquets. More than decoration, they give an amusing glimpse of what Romans expected from each other at a shared meal.
story.dinnerLine: “A Pompeii dining room has table-manner rules painted on the wall.”

sticker.title: Mind your manners
sticker.back: Painted rules told Roman guests how to behave at dinner.

story.recallPrompt: Remember the House of the Moralist? What advice was painted in its dining room?

sources.title: Board of Cultural Heritage of Pompeii (2015 guide, p. 43)
Wikipedia (it): Casa del Moralista

places.name: Bakery of Popidius Priscus
aiDescriptions: a Roman bakery with large hourglass-shaped stone mills and a domed brick oven
the bakery of Popidius Priscus in Pompeii

story.question: The big hourglass-shaped stones here did one job. What was it?
story.subtitle: Mills and oven under one roof.
story.body: This bakery brought grinding and baking together. Its stone mills turned grain into flour and its oven baked the bread: a Roman production line that fed the neighbourhood.
story.dinnerLine: “Pompeii’s bakers ground their own flour in big stone mills.”

sticker.title: Daily bread
sticker.back: Stone mills and an oven: a Roman bakery in one room.

story.recallPrompt: Remember the bakery’s hourglass stones? What did they do?

sources.title: Board of Cultural Heritage of Pompeii (2015 guide, p. 98)
